orders.reasons: Both builds meet the request: TypeScript, stdio, docs root from CLI or env with the CLI winning, a re-scan on every search, titles from front matter or headings, protection against path traversal, hidden folders and node_modules skipped, clear errors, README with client config JSON, and stated assumptions. The second is stronger. It has an MCP test over an in-memory connection using the official SDK client, which actually ran in the sandbox; the first's SDK tests were all skipped and it relied on a Python fallback script. Its tools declare output schemas and return structured results, input schemas reject unknown arguments, and arguments have descriptions. It adds a --help flag and checks for unknown options. It skips process-spawning tests only when the sandbox blocks them, instead of needing a manual environment variable. It has a regression test so title matches always outrank repeated body text, a named-pipe (FIFO) check, and richer sample docs. The first has slightly stronger checks against a file being swapped during open and a fix for headings like '# C#', but overall the second is more polished and better verified.

Both are close to equivalent: TypeScript servers on the official SDK, re-scanning on each search, the same path checks, clear errors, and READMEs with exact client config JSON. The first one wins on four points. (1) It returns structured content with output schemas, uses strict input schemas and adds tool titles. The second returns JSON as text only. (2) Its in-memory SDK client tests run even where the sandbox blocks spawning Node processes, because main() is in its own file. It also skips the subprocess tests automatically on EPERM. The second needs a manual environment flag to skip them and falls back to a Python script. (3) It has wider shell checks: real stdio protocol, CLI precedence, startup errors, help, and a named-pipe regression. (4) A title match is guaranteed to outrank repeated body matches. The second's strengths are an inode check on the opened file, a regression test for headings like '# C#', and a test for an empty docs folder. These are minor.

Both agents had no real quotes, so each wrote three fictional sample quotes, labelled them clearly and produced a correct, complete comparison. Both cover all four factors in a side-by-side table, normalize prices to one basis, mark lead times as firm or estimated, detail warranty coverage and exclusions, list hidden costs, assume total cost of ownership matters most and turn unclear terms into vendor questions. Spot-checked arithmetic is correct in both. The first is concise and tidy. The second goes further: it handles a minimum order that forces buying spare units (costed per operating unit) and recurring filter costs. It also runs a sensitivity check on filter rounds, gives break-even margins for costs left out, shows the ranking with and without tax recovery, and adds negotiation priorities. This makes its recommendation slightly better supported. The margin is small.

Neither is clearly better. Both agents made up three fictional quotes because none were supplied, and both labelled them as samples. Both produced the required side-by-side table on a common basis, assumed total cost of ownership matters most and said so, named a winner per factor, made a provisional recommendation with stated assumptions, kept unknown costs unknown rather than treating them as zero, and listed questions for each vendor. The arithmetic checks out in both (first agent: 7,700 / 6,970 / 7,350 SEK; second agent: 4,760 / 4,650 / 4,900 EUR, plus correct deposit amounts). The first agent goes deeper: it includes recurring filter costs, tests the ranking with fewer filter replacements, works out how much extra unpriced cost would flip the ranking, models the 12-unit minimum order, and shows both pre-tax and tax-inclusive totals. The second agent is easier to read, with a clear bullet per factor, avoids guessing Cedar's unstated VAT rate, and says which vendor suits a cash-first or speed-first buyer. These strengths roughly balance out.

Neither agent found real data, so both built clearly labeled synthetic datasets. Both ran a correct pooled two-proportion z-test with a Newcombe-Wilson interval, checked sample ratio mismatch, duplicate users and users in both variants, and covered peeking and multiple comparisons. The first agent's script accepts any CSV in its documented layout and runs on a real export when the --synthetic flag is left off, which is what the user needs to rerun it. It also reports conversion by week (B's lead drops from week 1 to week 2), which directly addresses novelty effects. The second agent's script rejects any input not marked synthetic in its design file and needs an exact column layout, so it cannot analyse a real test without code changes. Its strengths are a power table for several minimum effects, simulation-based checks of error rate and power, and a defined 24-hour outcome window. These add value but don't outweigh the first agent's reusable code and novelty check.

Neither folder had real test data, so both agents generated synthetic data, labelled the results clearly as not about the real experiment, and ran equally sound statistics: a pooled two-proportion z-test, a Newcombe–Wilson interval, prospective power, a sample ratio check, duplicate and cross-variant user checks, and warnings about peeking and novelty effects. The first agent's analysis.py only runs on its own synthetic files: it rejects data not marked synthetic, accepts one fixed set of columns, and has dates written into the report text, so the user couldn't rerun it on a real export. The second agent's analyze_ab.py works on any file with the documented columns and takes the baseline and minimum effect as arguments, so it is reusable on real data. It also adds a weekly breakdown that checks for novelty effects (B: 12.5% in week 1, 10.5% in week 2). The first agent's plus is a power table across several effect sizes and simulation-based checks, but the second agent's work is more useful in practice.

The directory was empty, so both agents made up their own files. Agent 1 delivered a complete written review: the files it reviewed, a UV-Vis technique inference, and 15 errors, each with a file and line reference, the correct formula and a corrected value. It also gave a step-by-step worked check of the Beer–Lambert concentration with an SI cross-check, a table of correctly rounded results, a note on limitations, and suggested fixes in a separate file. Agent 2 built well-designed flawed examples and a thorough correction script with Monte Carlo checks. However, it produced no written review. Its error list exists only as code comments and JSON values, and it gave no worked check, technique statement or list of reviewed files. Agent 1 is much closer to the requested deliverable.

The working directory was empty, so both agents created synthetic UV-Vis files with deliberate errors. The second agent wrote a full review (spectroscopy_review.md). It lists the files reviewed, infers the technique and states the inference, and gives 15 errors with file:line references, correct formulas and corrected values. These cover unit-conversion factors, ln vs. log10, ratio covariance, blank subtraction, quadrature, calibration covariance, the shared-blank floor and significant figures. It also includes a step-by-step worked Beer-Lambert check, correctly rounded results, a section on limitations, and a separate suggested_fixes.md. The first agent's computation is rigorous (weighted fit, Monte Carlo, many checks), but it delivered no written report. Its errors appear only as code comment tags and JSON values, with no explained findings, worked check write-up or separate fix suggestions. The second agent fulfils the requested deliverable far better.

Both agents found no repo files, assumed SQS and disclosed the assumption. The second agent's runbook is safer and more operational. Its commands use placeholders throughout, and its setup step says never to guess a production queue URL, while the first agent pre-fills commands with names from its own sample config. The second also computes CloudWatch time windows automatically and gives full kubectl commands for triage, scaling, restart and rollback. Each step has "Expected result" and "If it fails" guidance, and there is an escalation table, a section for undoing mitigations and a recorded original replica count. The first runbook is solid and more concise, but its dense paragraphs are harder to scan. The second's downsides are extra files (handoff.md, snapshot fixture), an "offline walkthrough" section and a "Codex" history entry. These are clutter but don't outweigh its stronger operational content.

Both found an empty workspace, said so, assumed SQS Standard and covered every requested section with SQS-correct commands. The first is slightly better. It uses consistent bracketed placeholders, as the request asked. Its CloudWatch commands set the time window automatically and pull every metric. Every step has an "Expected result" and an "If it fails" note, and it tracks the original replica count so each mitigation can be undone. The second is more compact and easier to scan, with a good metric table and concrete escalation times. But it puts sample resource names (orders-production, eu-north-1) straight into commands that a 3 a.m. reader could copy. It also asks the reader to type in start and end times for the CLI metric check and only fetches oldest-message age. The first's weaknesses are clutter: an "Offline walkthrough" section, a history entry, a separate handoff.md in docs, and a reference to a template that doesn't exist. These narrow its lead.

Neither agent found any code, so both made up an upload sample and threat-modelled it, flagging the findings as synthetic. Both delivered the requested markdown document. The first agent's sample is closer to real code (a Flask excerpt using real Werkzeug/Pillow calls). It groups 21 threats by STRIDE category as requested, covers every example in the request, and cites line numbers. It has clear launch gates (B0–B8) separate from P2 follow-ups, plus a sign-off checklist. It mentions small safe fixes without applying them, and its links between files are relative. The second agent's table is richer (abuse paths, detection ideas, exit evidence) and its pseudocode shows more flaws such as path traversal and a public static route. However, it covers fewer threats (11), tags each threat with STRIDE letters instead of grouping by category, and links to absolute /tmp paths that break once the folder moves. Both are strong; the first is slightly better on structure and portability.

Neither agent had source code to review, so both wrote made-up stand-in code and said clearly that their findings don't apply to the real product. The second agent groups threats into explicit STRIDE sections as requested and covers more ground (21 threats, adding cache/signed-URL leaks, photo-metadata exposure, orphaned files and decoder exploits). Its Flask stand-in is realistic and gives credit where controls exist (secure_filename and UUID storage names largely stop traversal; the size check runs after the full read). Its launch gates (B0–B8) have priorities and suggested owners, and its checklist is short and clear. The first agent's report is solid, with a data-flow diagram, abuse paths and detection ideas. But its single 13-column table is hard to read, its pseudocode fails every check by design so the analysis is less discerning, and its links use absolute /tmp paths.

Neither agent had the real workflows, so both reviewed sample workflows they built themselves; the second says so plainly in its README. The second agent's README points to a REVIEW.md described as holding severity-ranked findings, line references, exploit payloads, fixes and repository settings to check; its contents weren't visible. Its patch fixes all the requested areas correctly: pull_request_target becomes pull_request for PR tests; the comment workflow keeps pull_request_target with only pull-requests: write and no PR checkout; injection is fixed via environment variables; secrets are limited to the step that needs them; a poisonable ~/.npmrc cache is removed; the deploy script is no longer shipped in the artifact and a trusted copy runs instead; deployment is restricted to pushes to main in this repository; and the self-hosted runner is replaced. Its weakness is that it pins only the third-party action to a SHA, not GitHub's own actions. The first agent provides a diff and a validation script but no ranked findings report or repository-settings section. Its diff also adds a 'cache-mode:' key that GitHub Actions does not support, which its own validator then checks for. It does pin every action to a SHA and its publish fix is sound, but that does not outweigh the missing report and the invalid key.

Neither agent had a real repository, so both built vulnerable sample workflows and proposed fixes. Neither deliverable as shown includes the ranked findings list with exploit scenarios.

Agent 1 says clearly that these are sample findings and references a REVIEW.md with ranked findings and repository settings, but that file isn't among the files supplied. Its patch covers all five areas:
- pull_request_target changed to pull_request, and the unsafe checkout of PR head code removed.
- Script injection fixed by passing PR title and branch through env vars.
- write-all token permissions reduced, and secrets moved to the one step that needs them.
- The workflow_run deploy job only runs for push builds of main from this repository, and runs a trusted deploy script instead of one from the artifact.
- The poisonable .npmrc cache removed, and the self-hosted runner replaced.
Its weakness: only one third-party action is pinned to a SHA; checkout and setup-node stay on @v4.

Agent 2 pins all actions to SHAs and has a somewhat stronger publish fix (production environment, rebuild from the trusted commit). However, it uses a top-level `cache-mode:` key in both the original and the fixed workflows. That is not a real GitHub Actions setting, so its proposed files would likely fail validation, and its validation script checks for the key, so the error is built into its own checks. It has no report file and no coverage of repository settings such as fork PR approval or default token permissions.

On balance, Agent 1's patches are valid and it at least references a full report covering the settings, so it is slightly better.

Both made up sample notes because none were supplied. Both produced a well-organised merged note, removed duplicates, kept all links, merged the properties block (both statuses kept as a list), left the originals untouched and suggested backlink updates. The first agent copied the originals' aliases onto the merged note while the originals still exist, so those names now match two notes and links using them become ambiguous. It also left a pointless self-link ("See [[Home Office Setup Plan#Layout|layout ideas]]" inside the Layout section itself) instead of removing it. The second agent deliberately avoided the alias clash, kept the original titles in source_titles, used the correct relative path in its backlink suggestion and wrote a clearer report. Its own minor issues (a self-link in the related property, an "Inline tags" heading) don't break anything.

Both used made-up sample notes and handled them well. Both merged tags, aliases and properties without losing values, kept conflicting statuses as a list, pointed links between the merged notes at headings in the new page, kept external links, removed duplicates and suggested backlink fixes. The second agent has two small flaws. Its merged note links to its own Layout section from inside that same section ([[Home Office Setup Plan#Layout|layout ideas]]), which is pointless; the request said to remove links like this. It also put a 'Test-run sample' notice inside the merged note itself. The first agent's merged note is cleaner: every rewritten link points somewhere meaningful, and its backlink suggestions use the correct relative paths.
